description: Inputs, labels, and buttons — how pages collect information from visitors.

screens.body:
A <form> groups inputs that belong together — a login box, a signup box, a search bar. When the form is submitted, the browser gathers everything inside it and sends it off.

The action attribute says WHERE the data goes (a URL), and method says HOW (get or post). You'll wire these to a real backend later.

Even now, thinking in "forms" keeps related inputs organized instead of scattered across the page.

options: It groups related inputs for submission
It makes the inputs look nicer
It's required for every input on the page
check.question: What is a <form> for?

code.snippet:
<!-- display-only: grouping inputs -->
<form action="/signup" method="post">
  <!-- inputs go here -->
</form>

screens.heading: Forms group inputs together
screens.keyPoint: <form> wraps inputs that get submitted together. action = where, method = how.

screens.body:
<input> is the workhorse: one tag, many jobs. The type attribute picks the job — text, email, password, number, date, checkbox, and more.

The name attribute is the label the data gets when it's sent: name="email" means the server receives email=….

<input> never wraps content, so it's self-closing: <input type="text" name="username">.

check.question: Which is a correct email input?

code.snippet:
<!-- display-only: one tag, many jobs -->
<input type="text" name="username">
<input type="email" name="email">
<input type="password" name="password">

screens.heading: Inputs: one tag, many jobs
screens.keyPoint: type picks the job (text, email, password…); name labels the data for the server.

screens.body:
Every input deserves a <label>. It tells visitors what the field is for — and clicking the label focuses the input, which is a lovely touch on phones.

Connect them with a matching pair: the label's for attribute must equal the input's id.

Screen readers announce the label when the user reaches the field, so this isn't decoration — it's how many people understand your form.

check.question: Which label is correctly connected to its input?

code.snippet:
<!-- display-only: connected labels -->
<label for="email">Email address</label>
<input type="email" id="email" name="email">

screens.heading: Labels: every input's name tag
screens.keyPoint: label's for must match the input's id. Clicking the label focuses the field.

screens.body:
The type attribute does more than you think. type="email" checks for an @ on phones and shows the right keyboard; type="number" brings up a number pad.

type="password" hides what you type as dots. type="checkbox" and type="radio" make tick boxes and pick-one options.

Browsers do basic validation for free with the right type — one attribute, less JavaScript to write later.

options: type="email" — browsers validate the format for free
type="text" with a note saying "enter email"
check.question: Best type for an email field?

code.snippet:
<!-- display-only: types that help -->
<input type="email" name="email">
<input type="number" name="age" min="1" max="120">
<input type="checkbox" name="newsletter">

screens.heading: Input types that do the work
screens.keyPoint: Pick the right type and the browser validates + shows the right keyboard.

screens.body:
Buttons come in flavors via the type attribute. Inside a form, <button type="submit"> sends the form — that's the default, so an unlabeled <button> submits too.

<button type="button"> does NOTHING by itself — it's a blank slate for your JavaScript (like an "add another row" button).

Prefer <button> over <input type="submit">: buttons can hold text, icons, and styling, while inputs can only show plain text.

check.question: Which submits the form when clicked?

code.snippet:
<!-- display-only: button flavors -->
<button type="submit">Sign up</button>
<button type="button">Add another guest</button>
<button type="reset">Clear the form</button>

screens.heading: Buttons: submit vs plain
screens.keyPoint: type="submit" sends the form; type="button" is a blank slate for JavaScript.

screens.body:
Two more form friends. <textarea> is a multi-line text box — for messages, bios, reviews. It HAS a closing tag, and rows/cols set its size.

<select> makes a dropdown: it wraps <option> tags, one per choice. Add selected to pre-pick one.

Both need name attributes like inputs, and both deserve <label>s. Same rules, bigger boxes.

check.question: Which is right for a multi-line "Tell us about yourself" box?

code.snippet:
<!-- display-only: bigger inputs -->
<label for="bio">About you</label>
<textarea id="bio" name="bio" rows="4" cols="40"></textarea>

<label for="city">City</label>
<select id="city" name="city">
  <option>Calgary</option>
  <option selected>Edmonton</option>
</select>

screens.heading: Textareas and dropdowns

screens.body:
placeholder shows faint hint text inside an empty input ("you@example.com"). It's a hint, not a label — it vanishes the moment you type.

Never use placeholder INSTEAD of a label: once the user types, the hint is gone and they're guessing what the field was.

Use both: a real <label> for the name, a placeholder for an example. Accessible and helpful.

options: A <label>, because placeholders disappear when you type
A placeholder, because it's inside the box
Neither — the type attribute is enough
check.question: An email field needs a name users always see. Which?

code.snippet:
<!-- display-only: hint vs. label -->
<label for="email">Email address</label>
<input type="email" id="email" name="email"
       placeholder="you@example.com">

screens.heading: Placeholders are hints, not labels
screens.keyPoint: placeholder = faint example text. Always pair it with a real <label>.
